section_name: Step 1 Introduce — Organize into Provided Categories (K-2)
content:
REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information into provided categories (Grades K-2)

STEP 1 — INTRODUCE

"We've learned how to collect research from different sources. But we are still not ready to write our report. After collecting facts & details, writers execute a second prewriting step before writing their report— they ORGANIZE THE FACTS & DETAILS INTO GROUPS."

section_name: Step 2A Tell — Organize into Provided Categories (K-2)
content:
REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information into provided categories (Grades K-2)

STEP 2A — TELL THE CHILDREN — 5 MINUTES

WHY the skill is important: Before writing a report, writers organize their facts. Right now, our facts about different parts of the topic are all mixed up. If we wrote like this, our reader would get confused. We want to teach one part at a time so our report is easy to follow.

WHAT the skill is: "Organizing means putting facts that belong together into the same group. Think about a grocery store. Milk goes in dairy. Bread goes in bakery. Ice cream goes in frozen. The store doesn't mix everything on one shelf. Our research facts are the same way. When facts are about the same part of the topic, we say, 'These are all about _____.'' That group name is called a category."

"To sort our facts, we first need to separate them so we can move them around." (Show cut-apart facts.)

"We also need to know the category names. Just like a grocery store has dairy, bakery, and frozen, our report has category names, too." (In K-2, the teacher provides these.) "Then we sort the facts into the right groups—like a worker putting groceries in the correct section."

HOW the skill works:
1. Choose 1 category and say its name aloud.
2. Keep all the facts in one pile. Pick up one and read it. Ask yourself, "Does this fact belong in this category?" IF YES, say why it fits and place it under that category. IF NO, move it aside and read the next fact.
3. Keep reading through all the facts to find the ones that fit Category A. Then repeat the same process with Category B, rereading the leftover facts to see if they belong there. Continue until all the facts are sorted into the given categories.

"When we organize facts, we are NOT changing them and we are NOT adding new ones. We aren't even using our pencils. We are simply sorting the facts into the right groups."

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information into provided categories (Kindergarten)

STEP 2B — SHOW THE CHILDREN — 5 MINUTES

Topic: Space. Teacher demonstrates sorting previously collected research facts on Space into provided categories.

"Let me show you how I organize the research facts on Space that were previously collected from sources."

Point to the first category. "The first category is Earth. I say the category name over and over to help my brain stay on track: Earth... Earth... Earth."

Holding all the facts in a single stack, read aloud the one on top. Fact: "Earth = where we live." "Is this about Earth? Yes. It tells what Earth is. This fits the Earth category." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "Earth is always moving." "Is this about Earth? Yes. It tells something Earth does. It fits." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "rotates = spins." "I'm remembering when I wrote this fact. It was about how the Earth moves. Yes, it goes with the 'Earth' category." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "space is above Earth." "Hmmm... This fact has 'Earth' in it. But it's not about the Earth; it's about what is above it. It's about where space is— above the Earth. This does not teach me something about Earth itself. I'm going to move it aside." (Start a "leftover" fact pile for those that don't fit the category.)

Fact: "sun = star." "Is that about Earth? No, that's about the sun." (Add it to the leftover pile.)

Fact: "hard like rocks." "Hmm... The Earth is hard like rocks. But wait... other planets are hard and rocky, too. So this fact isn't just about Earth. It could also be about planets. Hmm... Sometimes a fact could fit in more than one group. And since it doesn't say 'Earth' on the note, I'm going to put it to the side for now." (Add it to the leftover pile.)

"This is how writers organize their facts for a report. When I finish checking all the facts for 'Earth,' I move to the next category—'Sun.' I reread the leftover facts and sort them again. I keep going until every fact is in a group."

"Careful thinkers don't rush. They don't just grab and place. They stop and think about where each fact fits best. When we sort our facts & details slowly and carefully, our report will be clear and easy to follow."

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information into provided categories (Kindergarten)

STEP 3 — INTERACT

Topic: Weather (different topic from Step 2B's Space).

Reveal categories & researched facts on Weather that were previously collected from sources. Show these facts & categories on XL slips of paper/sticky notes.

Guide students through a series of Turn & Talks to organize the facts under the different categories.

"When you finish reading all the research facts for one category, then move onto the next category."

section_name: Step 4 Close — Organize into Provided Categories (K-2)
content:
REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information into provided categories (Grades K-2)

STEP 4 — CLOSE

"Writers, today we learned how to organize our research facts into categories. This is the second step to prewriting before drafting a report."

"During Independent Writing Time, you will work with a partner to sort facts about (TOPIC) into the categories I will give you. Make sure that you don't just sort the facts quickly to be done. Work together and talk through each research fact to determine if it fits that category. Put it under that category label— or set it to the side."

"Let's go be writers!"

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information into provided categories (Grade 1)

STEP 2B — SHOW THE CHILDREN — 5 MINUTES

Topic: US Symbols. Teacher demonstrates sorting previously collected research facts on US Symbols into provided categories (American flag, Bald Eagle, Statue of Liberty, White House).

"Let me show you how I organize the research facts on US Symbols that were previously collected from sources."

Point to the first category. "The first category is American flag. I say the category name over and over to help my brain stay on track: American flag... American flag... American flag."

Holding all the facts in a single stack, read aloud the one on top. Fact: "13 stripes = 13 states." "Is this about the American flag? Yes! The flag has stripes. This fact says what the stripes stand for. It fits." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "50 stars = 50 states." "Is this about the American flag? Yes. Stars are on the flag. This tells what the stars mean. It fits." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "blue square = field." "This is another fact about the flag— about the blue part. That helps describe what the flag looks like. It fits under American flag." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "National bird." "Hmm... There isn't a bird on our flag. That doesn't go with American flag— it's about the bald eagle." (Start a "leftover" fact pile.)

Fact: "strength & freedom." "Hmm... I remember that many U.S. symbols stand for strength and freedom. That could match the American flag—but it could also match the bald eagle. Sometimes a fact fits more than one group. Since it doesn't say 'flag,' I'm not sure yet. I'll put it to the side for now." (Add it to the leftover pile.)

Fact: "not touch ground." "Is that about the American flag? Yes—this is a flag rule. It tells us how to treat the flag— with respect. It fits." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "symbol = stands for something." "Hmm... It helps explain what the flag is—a symbol." (Start to move it.) "But wait... lots of things are symbols. It might fit other groups, too. Since I'm not completely sure, I'll set it aside and decide later." (Add it to the leftover pile.)

"This is how writers organize their facts for a report. When I finish checking the facts for 'American flag,' I move to the next category—'Bald Eagle.' I reread the leftover facts and sort them again. I keep going until every fact is in a group."

"Careful thinkers don't rush. They don't just grab and place. They stop and think about where each fact fits best. When we sort our facts & details slowly and carefully, our report will be clear and easy to follow."

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information into provided categories (Grade 1)

STEP 3 — INTERACT

Topic: Space (different topic from Step 2B's US Symbols).

Reveal categories & researched facts on Space that were previously collected from sources. Show these facts & categories on XL slips of paper/sticky notes.

Guide students through a series of Turn & Talks to organize the facts under the different categories.

"When you finish reading all the research facts for one category, then move onto the next category."

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information into provided categories (Grade 2)

STEP 2B — SHOW THE CHILDREN — 5 MINUTES

Topic: Public Services. Teacher demonstrates sorting previously collected research facts on Public Services into provided categories (Recreation, Roads, Public Safety, Knowledge Building).

"Let me show you how I organize the research facts on Public Services that were previously collected from sources."

Point to the first category: Recreation. "I say the category name over and over to help my brain stay on track: Recreation... Recreation... Recreation."

Holding all the facts in a single stack, read aloud the one on top. Fact: "families— play & exercise." "Is this about recreation? Yes. Recreation is when families play and exercise. It fits." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "open to community." "Is this about recreation? Yes. Recreation places are open to everyone. It fits." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "relax, move, spend time." "Is this about recreation? Yes. These are things people do during recreation. It fits." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "public services." "Is this about recreation? Well... recreation is one of the public services—but this fact is not ONLY about recreation. Sometimes a fact fits more than one group. Since it doesn't fit 'recreation' specifically, I'll put it to the side for now." (Start a "leftover" fact pile.)

Fact: "libraries— books to borrow." "Is this about recreation? Well... some people read for fun, but this is mostly about the books, which are at libraries. That's a different public service— not recreation." (Add it to the leftover pile.)

Fact: "sports fields— soccer & baseball." "Is this about recreation? Yes. Playing sports, like soccer & baseball, is recreation. It fits." (Place under the category label.)

Fact: "parks & playgrounds— safe." "Is this about recreation? Hmm... safety is also about police and firefighters. But the research note includes 'parks and playgrounds' on it. So I'm thinking it's more about how these recreational areas are safe for the community. So I'm thinking it fits under recreation." (Place under the category label.)

"This is how writers organize their facts for a report. When I finish checking the facts for 'Recreation' I move to the next category—'Roads.' I reread the leftover facts and sort them again. I keep going until every fact is in a group."

"Careful thinkers don't rush. They don't just grab and place. They stop and think about where each fact fits best. When we sort our facts & details slowly and carefully, our report will be clear and easy to follow."

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information into provided categories (Grade 2)

STEP 3 — INTERACT

Topic: Habitats (different topic from Step 2B's Public Services).

Reveal categories & researched facts on Habitats that were previously collected from sources. Show these facts & categories on XL slips of paper/sticky notes.

Guide students through a series of Turn & Talks to organize the facts under the different categories.

"When you finish reading all the research facts for one category, then move onto the next category."

section_name: Step 1 Introduce — Organize to Create Own Categories (3-5)
content:
REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information to create your own categories (Grades 3-5)

STEP 1 — INTRODUCE

"We've learned how to collect research from different sources. But we are still not ready to write our report. After collecting facts & details, writers execute a second prewriting step before writing their report— they ORGANIZE THE FACTS & DETAILS INTO GROUPS."

section_name: Step 2A Tell — Organize to Create Own Categories (3-5)
content:
REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information to create your own categories (Grades 3-5)

STEP 2A — TELL THE CHILDREN — 5 MINUTES

WHAT the skill is: "Organizing means grouping related facts into categories. A category is a short label that names what a group of facts is mostly about. Think of a grocery store: dairy, bakery, frozen. Items are sorted by what they are. Report writing works the same way—facts about the same part of the topic belong together."

WHY the skill is important: "But, right now, our research notes are in the order we collected them—not the order we should teach them. If we start writing with mixed-up facts, our reader will be confused. Consequently, we need to sort our research facts into the right groups—like a worker putting individual groceries in the correct sections of the store."

"To help us see which details belong together, we use colors." (Reveal highlighters, crayons, markers.) "Each color will stand for a new category—a different part of the report."

HOW the skill works — Detail the process:
1. Read one fact from the bulleted list & ask "What part of the topic is this about?"
2. Hunt for a match. Reread each research note and look for facts that connect.
3. Mark both facts with the same color and name the category.
4. Continue reading facts, marking those that fit that same category.

When one category is complete, return to the unmarked facts and look for a new connection. Form a second category, then a third, and possibly a fourth—each time rereading the leftover facts to see what goes together.

TIP 1: There isn't one "right" way to group facts. Categories often focus on parts, people, places, types, steps, cause and effect, what something is, what it does, or why it matters.

TIP 2: Some facts may never form a strong group. They may be true, but without enough related details, they won't be used in this report.

"After researching and collecting facts, writers organize them into categories. Accuracy in report writing isn't just about true facts; it's also about grouping related facts together so the report is clear and easy to understand."

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information to create your own categories (Grade 3)

STEP 2B — SHOW THE CHILDREN — 5 MINUTES

Topic: Simple Machines. Teacher demonstrates creating categories by reading research notes and color-coding related facts.

"Let me show you how I organize the research facts previously collected on Simple Machines. I start by reading a fact at the top of my research notes."

Read "Simple machines (arrow) work easier." (Translate it as "Simple machines make work easier.") "I ask myself 'What is this about?' It states the overall purpose of simple machines. Now I don't mark anything yet. I keep reading to find a connected or related fact that matches."

Read "lift/move/push heavy objects." (Translate it as "Simple machines work by lifting, moving, or pushing heavy objects.") "Is this about the overall purpose of simple machines? Yes! I've found a second related detail."

"I'm going to mark both the first and second fact with the same color. Now I need to jot down a phrase that labels this group of facts. Since I said 'overall purpose' when I was explaining what each one was about, it makes sense that would be my label." Now I have 2 facts on the purpose of simple machines. I'm hunting for a third.

(The next several research notes are about specific types of simple machines. Think aloud about how they are NOT facts universal to all simple machines, so they don't fit the category you've started.)

Read "Simple machines (arrow) safer/easier work." (Translate.) "OK, this is about all simple machines. In general, they all make work easier and safer. This fits the overall purpose of simple machines, so I'm marking it with the first color. It fits that category."

Read "Simple machines = force tools." (Translate.) "Again, this is about all simple machines. They are tools that use force to work. This is another general or overall fact. I'm marking this one, too."

Read "Force = push or pull." (Translate.) "This explains how all simple machines work. I'm marking it."

Read "No motors/engines." (Translate.) "This describes another overall or general characteristic. I'm marking it."

Read "Work bc shape & design." (Translate.) "This fits, too. It's a general feature of all simple machines. Mark it."

Read "Lever: fulcrum (arrow) less effort." (Translate.) "OK, now this fact is specific to levers. It does not fit overall purpose of ALL simple machines. I'm leaving it unmarked."

"This is how writers notice related facts and group information in categories. After finishing one category, reread the remaining facts to form another and another. Let's try the next one together."

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information to create your own categories (Grade 3)

STEP 3 — INTERACT

Topic: Fossils (different topic from Step 2B's Simple Machines).

Project researched facts on Fossils that were previously collected from sources. Guide students through a series of Turn & Talks to organize the facts into categories.

section_name: Step 4 Close — Organize to Create Own Categories (3-5)
content:
REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information to create your own categories (Grades 3-5)

STEP 4 — CLOSE

"Writers, today we learned how to group our research facts into categories. This is the second step to prewriting before drafting a report."

"During Independent Writing Time, you will work with a partner to highlight related research facts about (TOPIC). Work together and talk through each research fact to determine what it means and what it belongs with. Use highlighters to reveal the grouped facts and name the categories they fit under."

"It's possible that some of your research facts will not be highlighted as they do not fit under a broader category."

"Let's go be writers!"

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information to create your own categories (Grade 4)

STEP 2B — SHOW THE CHILDREN — 5 MINUTES

Topic: Ben Franklin. Teacher demonstrates creating categories by reading research notes and color-coding related facts.

"Let me show you how I organize the research facts previously collected on Ben Franklin. I start by reading a fact at the top of my research notes."

Read "Ben Franklin = key early Am. leader." (Translate it as "Ben Franklin was a key early American leader.") "I ask myself 'What is this about?' It describes who Benjamin Franklin was— an important leader in America. Now I don't mark anything yet. I keep reading to find a connected or related fact."

Read "born 1706 — Boston." (Translate it as "Ben Franklin was born in 1706 in Boston.") "Is this about his leadership? No. It's a biographical detail — when & where he was born. I'm only looking for details that describe Ben as a leader. Since this doesn't match the category, I'm leaving it unmarked."

Read "writer, inventor, scientist, statesman." (Translate it as "Ben Franklin was a writer, inventor, scientist, and statesman.") "This is definitely about who Ben Franklin was, about his leadership, & the roles he played. I've found a second related detail."

"I'm going to mark both the first and third fact with the same color. Now I need to jot down a phrase that labels this group of facts. Since I said words like 'role' and 'leader' I'm thinking that should be part of the label: 'Roles he played—a leader.' Now I have 2 facts on who Ben Franklin was. I'm hunting for a third."

Read "published Poor Richard's Almanack." (Translate.) "This is about something specific he did when he was young. I guess it's a role or job he had, but not one where he was a leader. I'm leaving it unmarked."

Read "believed in learning + sharing knowledge." (Translate.) "This fact describes Ben's character, his personality. It explains something about who he was and what guided his work. That fits the bigger idea of his leadership and influence. I'm marking this one."

(The next several research notes are about the kite, lightning, electricity, discoveries. Think aloud about how they are about one experiment and its results—not Ben's overall character or leadership role. So I leave them unmarked.)

Read "cared about community improvement." (Translate.) "This is not about one invention. This is about his character and values. Yes — that fits the idea of his overall leadership and influence. I'm marking it."

"This is how writers organize their facts. After finishing one category, I reread the remaining facts to form another and another. Let's try the next one together."

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information to create your own categories (Grade 4)

STEP 3 — INTERACT

Topic: European Exploration (different topic from Step 2B's Ben Franklin).

Project researched facts on European Exploration that were previously collected from sources. Guide students through a series of Turn & Talks to organize the facts into categories.

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information to create your own categories (Grade 5)

STEP 2B — SHOW THE CHILDREN — 5 MINUTES

Topic: Paul Revere. Teacher demonstrates creating categories by reading research notes and color-coding related facts.

"Let me show you how I organize the research facts previously collected on Paul Revere. I start by reading a fact at the top of my research notes."

Read "Paul Revere = leader (Am. Revolution)." "I ask myself, What is this about? Well, it tells me he was a leader during the American Revolution. That sounds like a big, overall idea about the role he played. Now I don't mark anything yet. I keep reading to find a connected or related fact that matches."

Read "revolution = fight to change gov't." (Translate it as "The revolution was a fight to change who their government was.") "Is this about Paul Revere's leadership or his overall role? No. It's background information; it just defines the word revolution. I'm leaving it unmarked. I'm only looking for details that fit the category of Paul Revere & his role as a leader."

Read "supported colonies' independence." (Translate it as "Someone supported the colonies', the colonists' independence.") "That was Paul Revere! That's what he did. Yes. This fact is about his role in the fight for freedom."

"I'm going to mark both the first and third fact with the same color. Now I need to jot down a phrase that labels this group of facts. Since I said words like 'role' and 'leader' I'm thinking that should be part of the label— 'Role as a leader.' Now I have 2 facts on what Paul Revere did. I'm hunting for a third."

Read "believed colonies self-govern." (Translate it as "Someone believes the colonies should govern themselves.") "This is another fact that explains what Paul Revere believed as a leader. I'm going to mark it."

Read "worked to support freedom." (Translate.) "Yes. This continues the same idea. I'm going to mark it."

Read "joined secret groups." (Translate.) "Does this explain Paul Revere's role? Yes — joining secret groups shows how he acted on his beliefs. I'm going to mark it."

Read "spy = gather British intel." (Translate.) "This shows a specific action he took. It fits under his role as a leader in the American Revolution. I'm going to mark it."

Read "Sons of Liberty member." (Translate.) "Yes — this is one of the spy groups Paul Revere was in. I'm going to mark it."

Read "groups met quietly (arrow) plan protests/share info." (Translate it as "Groups met quietly to plan protests and share information.") "Well, I'm sure Paul Revere led some of those groups, but this is about the colonists and how they worked together. I'm leaving this one unmarked."

"This is how writers organize their facts. After finishing one category, I reread the remaining facts to form another and another. Let's try the next one together."

REPORT WRITING SKILL #2: Organize information to create your own categories (Grade 5)

STEP 3 — INTERACT

Topic: Earth's Spheres (different topic from Step 2B's Paul Revere).

Project researched facts on Earth's Spheres that were previously collected from sources. Guide students through a series of Turn & Talks to organize the facts into categories.

section_name: Skill 2 Overview — Two Variants by Grade Band
content:
REPORT WRITING SKILL #2 OVERVIEW: Organize information into categories (K-5)

Skill 2 is the second prewriting step in report writing, following Skill 1 (collect facts & details from sources). After collecting research, writers organize their facts into groups before drafting.

This skill has two grade-band variants:

- Grades K-2: "Organize information into PROVIDED categories." The teacher gives students the category names. Students sort cut-apart facts into the given categories by physically placing facts under category labels. The process is: choose one category, say its name aloud, read each fact and ask "Does this belong in this category?" — place it if yes, set aside if no. Repeat for each category.

- Grades 3-5: "Organize information to CREATE YOUR OWN categories." Students derive their own category names by reading research notes, hunting for related facts, color-coding matches with highlighters, and labeling each group. The process is: read a fact, ask "What part of the topic is this about?", hunt for a matching fact, mark both with the same color, name the category, and continue. Some facts may not fit any category.

Key pedagogical points shared across all grades:
- Organizing is NOT changing or adding facts — just sorting them into groups.
- Careful thinkers don't rush; they stop and think about where each fact fits best.
- Sometimes a fact could fit more than one group — set it aside and decide later.
- After finishing one category, reread the leftover facts and form the next category.
- The goal is a clear, easy-to-follow report where related facts are grouped together.

Step 2B topics by grade: K = Space, 1 = US Symbols, 2 = Public Services, 3 = Simple Machines, 4 = Ben Franklin, 5 = Paul Revere.
Step 3 topics by grade: K = Weather, 1 = Space, 2 = Habitats, 3 = Fossils, 4 = European Exploration, 5 = Earth's Spheres.
